Opening

BUILD · SCIENCE · W9A · 2 MINUTES

Rock Evidence Lab: Look Before You Label

Learning objective

I can compare coded rocks using observations and apply a clear grouping rule.

Success looks like

  • Describe two visible features.
  • Compare two specimens using the same feature.
  • State a rule and use it consistently.

Your team has a tray of unnamed rock models. Build a useful description before anyone guesses the name.

W9A · one 40-minute lesson

Seven stages, with one arrival and one exit. Use the route that helps you show your science today.

No earlier worksheet is needed. Fresh evidence is included.

Point, speak, sign, move cards, draw, write or direct an adult. Use one response mode; no separate participation form.

Arrival

BUILD · SCIENCE · W9A · 5 MINUTES

Four clues to start

Choose a route. Four checks help your teacher decide what support is useful today.

Supported · 4 questions

1. Look

Code A shows crystals. Point to the feature: crystals or favourite?

Help beside the question
Use the supplied feature card.

Answer guidance

Answer: Crystals.

2. Word

Which is a property: rough or best?

Help beside the question
A property can be observed or tested.

Answer guidance

Answer: Rough.

3. Sort

A rule is “has visible holes”. Does Code F belong in YES?

Help beside the question
F has many visible holes.

Answer guidance

Answer: Yes.

4. Care

Must you touch a rock to describe its picture?

Help beside the question
Pointing or directing is valid.

Answer guidance

Answer: No.

Standard · 4 questions

1. Describe

Give one observation from Code A.

Help beside the question
Use “I can see…”

Answer guidance

Answer: Visible interlocking crystals.

2. Compare

What differs between A and C?

Help beside the question
Compare their visible surface features.

Answer guidance

Answer: A shows crystals; C shows sand-sized grains and faint bands.

3. Rule

Why state the grouping rule first?

Help beside the question
Think consistency.

Answer guidance

Answer: So the same criterion is applied to each sample.

4. Claim

Does grey colour prove a rock name?

Help beside the question
Separate description from identity.

Answer guidance

Answer: No.

Stretch · 4 questions

1. Observation

How does “visible crystals” differ from “must be granite”?

Help beside the question
One describes; one identifies.

Answer guidance

Answer: The first is a checkable observation; the second is an identity claim.

2. Groups

Can two different groupings both work?

Help beside the question
Name the rule each uses.

Answer guidance

Answer: Yes, with different clear criteria.

3. Limit

Name one limitation of a specimen picture.

Help beside the question
Think scale, lighting or hidden properties.

Answer guidance

Answer: It may obscure scale or features and cannot establish hidden properties.

4. Transfer

Does grouping by holes measure water passage?

Help beside the question
A visible hole is not a controlled flow test.

Answer guidance

Answer: No.

Starter

BUILD · SCIENCE · W9A · 4 MINUTES

Two grey rocks: the same group?

Two rocks look grey. Is colour enough for every useful grouping?

No answer chosen yet. Think or discuss first.

I do

BUILD · SCIENCE · W9A · 7 MINUTES

Make the science visible

Predict, model, explain

I can see __ in Code __. My grouping rule is __.

Choose each view. Describe the evidence before giving a conclusion.

Keep the specimen code. Notice visible features before guessing a rock name.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

The drawings are schematic feature models, not photographs or identification keys. Visible colour, bands and grains may vary with lighting, weathering and the specimen. A visible grouping does not prove mineral content, hardness or permeability.

Local explainer · 32 seconds · silent with captions

Use instead of part of the demonstration. It never autoplays and needs no internet.

Full text / no-video alternative

00–08 seconds · Look before naming
Keep the specimen code. Notice visible features before guessing a rock name.

08–16 seconds · Compare the same feature
Code A has visible crystals. Code C has grains and faint bands. Both are observations.

16–24 seconds · Choose a clear rule
Ask: are bands or flat planes visible? Say exactly what YES means before sorting.

24–32 seconds · Keep the boundary
The grouping describes these supplied views. It does not prove the names of all unknown rocks.

Use the supplied diagrams or teacher-screened educational specimens on trays. No throwing, tasting, smelling, breaking, grinding or dust blowing. Touching a rock is optional. Wash hands after any handling.

We do

BUILD · SCIENCE · W9A · 10 MINUTES

Use the evidence together

Use a clue; explain the group

Select a card, then select its group. Keyboard, pointing and paper routes work too. You can move a card when your reasoning changes.

Visible crystals

Visible grains

Bands / flat planes

Large holes

No large feature in this view

Select a card, then choose a group.

Would a small change help? · optional

You may ask for a clearer diagram, fewer cards at once, reading help or more thinking time. Tell your teacher, ask privately, point or pass. Your teacher will say what can change and check whether it helped. No extra sheet is needed.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

Accept observations consistent with the cards. A and C both show visible components, but crystals differ from grains. Apply the chosen rule consistently.

You do

BUILD · SCIENCE · W9A · 10 MINUTES

Show your science

Use today’s evidence

Fresh evidence desk

Choose the digital choices or matching paper. You do not need to complete both.

Supplied teaching models and coded observations. These are not measurements collected by this class. Codes refer only to this lesson’s evidence set.

CodeSupplied visible evidence
ASpeckled surface with visible interlocking crystals.
BDark fine-looking surface; no large grains, holes or bands visible.
CMany sand-sized grains and faint bands; use grains as the strongest feature here.
DPale fine-looking surface; no large crystals or holes visible.
EClear flat, sheet-like planes.
FMany large visible holes.
TVisible bands; no large crystals or holes in this view.
Choose two coded views.
Describe the same features on each.
State one observable grouping rule.
Apply it and explain a placement.

Supported · build your explanation

1. Notice

Use A and F. Point to one feature of each.

Help: Crystals / holes.

2. Compare

Show one difference between A and F.

Help: A has __; F has __.

3. Group

Use “visible holes”: place A and F.

Help: Say the rule before moving.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

A shows crystals; F shows holes. Under the holes rule F is YES and A is NO.

Standard · build your explanation

1. Inspect

Record two features across A, C and E.

Help: Use only visible evidence.

2. Compare

Compare A and C using the same feature words.

Help: One similarity and one difference.

3. Classify

Group all seven views with one yes/no rule.

Help: Write the rule first; use an uncertain group if needed.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

Accept observations consistent with the cards. A and C both show visible components, but crystals differ from grains. Apply the chosen rule consistently.

Stretch · build your explanation

1. Two rules

Group the cards once by holes and once by bands/planes.

Help: Keep each definition fixed.

2. Explain

Choose a card that changes group and explain why.

Help: The rule changed, not the specimen.

3. Limit

State what neither grouping can establish.

Help: Names or hidden test properties.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

For holes: F yes, the other supplied views no. For bands/planes: C, E and T yes; A, B, D and F no. Neither proves identity.

Observation or claim?

Use the digital choices or the matching paper page. One response mode is enough.

Revisit the model

Keep the specimen code. Notice visible features before guessing a rock name.

Refine one explanation

Check that the explanation follows the supplied observation and keeps the stated limit.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

Accept observations consistent with the cards. A and C both show visible components, but crystals differ from grains. Apply the chosen rule consistently.

Exit

BUILD · SCIENCE · W9A · 2 MINUTES

Two small checks

Supported · 2 questions

1. Observe

Which is an observation: visible bands or best rock?

Help beside the question
Choose what can be seen.

Answer guidance

Answer: Visible bands.

2. Rule

Does F fit “visible holes”?

Help beside the question
Read F’s clue.

Answer guidance

Answer: Yes.

Standard · 2 questions

1. Compare

Give one difference between A and E.

Help beside the question
Crystals / flat planes.

Answer guidance

Answer: A has visible crystals; E has flat planes.

2. Limit

Does the grouping prove each rock name?

Help beside the question
Use observation versus identity.

Answer guidance

Answer: No.

Stretch · 2 questions

1. Regroup

Could F move when the rule changes?

Help beside the question
Apply the new criterion consistently.

Answer guidance

Answer: Yes; membership depends on the stated rule.

2. Evidence

Why avoid naming from colour alone?

Help beside the question
One feature is insufficient.

Answer guidance

Answer: Different rocks can share colours, and appearance varies.

Knowledge organiser

BUILD Science · W9A · Shared resource

Learning objective

I can compare coded rocks using observations and apply a clear grouping rule.

Key words

property — A feature we can observe or test.

observe — Notice and record without guessing a name.

classify — Put into groups using a stated rule.

specimen — One sample being examined.

Remember

  • Look for crystals, grains, bands, flat planes or holes.
  • Colour alone does not prove a rock name.
  • Different clear rules can create different valid groups.
  • A picture cannot establish hidden properties.

Success looks like

  • Describe two visible features.
  • Compare two specimens using the same feature.
  • State a rule and use it consistently.

I can see __ in Code __. My grouping rule is __.

Current stage

Preparation and access

Use the supplied diagrams or teacher-screened educational specimens on trays. No throwing, tasting, smelling, breaking, grinding or dust blowing. Touching a rock is optional. Wash hands after any handling.

Scientific care

The drawings are schematic feature models, not photographs or identification keys. Visible colour, bands and grains may vary with lighting, weathering and the specimen. A visible grouping does not prove mineral content, hardness or permeability.

Responsive feedback within teaching

The lesson teacher hears an optional request, explains what can change, tries it and checks the effect. Passing or asking privately is valid. No compulsory participation task or new pupil form. Do not infer assessment codes from a click, download or written box.

BUILD Science · Sugar Evidence: Read the Label · Supported

Your task

1. Use these fictional teaching cards. All give sugar in g per 100 g: A — 4 g; B — 9 g; C — 14 g; D — 23 g.

Help with this question

Use a paper strip to track one card at a time. Say or point to the letter, the sugar number and ‘g per 100 g’ together.

2. Put the four cards in order from LEAST sugar per 100 g to MOST. Point, move paper cards or direct an adult.

Help with this question

Compare two numbers first. Place the smaller one towards LEAST, then find where each remaining card belongs.

3. Complete: Label ___ has the least sugar per 100 g. Label ___ has the most.

Help with this question

Look at the two ends of your own order. Use those card letters to fill the gaps.

4. Choose the claim we can support: 'A has less sugar per 100 g than D' / 'A is the healthiest food for everyone'.

Help with this question

Ask: does this sentence describe the sugar evidence, or claim to know everything about the food?

5. Finish or point: These sugar numbers show ONE PART OF NUTRITION / THE WHOLE EATING PATTERN. Keep “g per 100 g” with each number.

Help with this question

Look at what was measured. Think about whether these cards show every nutrient and everything a person eats.

BUILD Science · Sugar Evidence: Read the Label · Standard

Your task

1. Read these fictional teaching labels. Each is PER 100 g. A: carbohydrate 22 g; of which sugars 4 g. B: carbohydrate 67 g; of which sugars 9 g. C: carbohydrate 58 g; of which sugars 14 g. D: carbohydrate 72 g; of which sugars 23 g.

Help with this question

Track the ‘of which sugars’ row. Keep the carbohydrate and sugar rows separate.

2. Make a results row for each label. Copy the SUGAR value with its unit and basis; do not copy total carbohydrate.

Help with this question

Use the headings Label | Sugar / g per 100 g. Check each copied value against its nutrient name.

3. Order A–D from least to most sugar per 100 g.

Help with this question

Check adjacent pairs: is each value no larger than the next? Recheck that all four use the same basis.

4. Write or say one comparison: 'Label ___ has ___ g sugar per 100 g. This is less/more than ___.'

Help with this question

Build the comparison from two complete readings. Include which label you are comparing it with.

5. Explain one thing these sugar numbers cannot tell us about the whole food or eating pattern.

Help with this question

Choose one missing piece of information. Explain why that missing information limits a wider judgement.

BUILD Science · Sugar Evidence: Read the Label · Stretch

Your task

1. Fictional labels, all PER 100 g: A — carbohydrate 22 g, sugars 4 g; B — carbohydrate 67 g, sugars 9 g; C — carbohydrate 58 g, sugars 14 g; D — carbohydrate 72 g, sugars 23 g.

Help with this question

Identify the nutrient and reference amount before selecting numerical evidence.

2. Extract the four sugar values and order them. Keep the unit and basis.

Help with this question

Audit the completed order against the source labels; a correct number copied from the wrong row is still the wrong evidence.

3. Extra label E says 'sugars 3 g per 25 g serving'. Someone puts E before A because 3 is less than 4. Audit this decision.

Help with this question

Compare the reference quantities before comparing the two bare numbers.

4. Put E on a per-100 g basis before comparing. How many 25 g servings make 100 g? Then place E among A–D.

Help with this question

Find the scale factor from 25 g of food to 100 g of food. Apply the same factor to the sugar amount.

5. Write one supported comparison from A–D and repair this claim: 'The lowest-sugar card proves the best food for everybody.'

Help with this question

Separate a justified numerical comparison from a wider judgement. State exactly what the evidence establishes and what it leaves unknown.
